pulls: Jesus does not begin the prayer with ‘give me.’ He begins it with ‘Our Father.’ Before a forgiven man asks God for anything, he remembers who he is talking to — and whose he is.
paras: A man accounted righteous by faith, standing on Christ’s finished work, has one thing left to learn: how to talk to the God who declared him so. And it begins exactly where it should — not with techniques, but with the disciples watching Jesus pray and asking the only sensible question: Lord, teach us to pray. They had prayed their whole lives. They were religious men. And still they knew that whatever Jesus was doing when He prayed, they did not know how to do it. So they asked. And He answered, not with a lecture, but with a prayer — the prayer, the one He gave the church to pray and to be shaped by forever.

Notice first that Jesus assumes a man will pray. He does not say if you pray, but when you pray. Prayer is not an elite discipline for spiritual athletes; it is the breathing of a forgiven son. And notice second where the prayer begins — not with the man’s needs, but with God. Our Father in heaven. May your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done. Three petitions about God before a single petition about the man. The prayer Jesus teaches reorders a man’s whole inner world before it ever gets to his daily bread.

This week sits with the opening of the prayer: the address that changes everything (Our Father in heaven), and the first three petitions, all of them aimed at God — His name, His kingdom, His will. Martin Luther, who prayed this prayer his whole life, wrote to his barber that he still nursed at it like a child and never got his fill. Enter it the same way — not to recite it faster, but to be slowly remade by it.

sections.heading: WHAT WE ARE GOING AFTER
paras: This week goes after the reordering the Lord’s Prayer works in a man’s heart — the way it lifts his eyes off himself before it ever lets him mention himself. Most men, left to themselves, pray a list: fix this, provide that, protect them, help me. Jesus does not forbid the list; He puts it second. First comes the Father, the Name, the Kingdom, the Will. The prayer trains a man to want God’s glory, God’s reign, and God’s will before his own comfort — and in doing so it heals the very self-centeredness that keeps a soul in the dust.

The goal this week is to learn to pray the first half of the prayer as more than words — to mean Our Father as a forgiven son, to long for the Name to be kept holy, the Kingdom to come, the Will to be done. A man who has walked the gospel can pray Our Father with a weight he could not before: he is not approaching a distant judge but a Father who, having laid his iniquity on the Servant, now welcomes him home. Prayer is built on the gospel. A man prays as a son because the gospel made him one.

sections.heading: WHY START HERE
paras: Because a man who has just been declared righteous needs, more than anything, to learn how to talk to the God who declared it — and he will get it wrong if he starts with himself. Beginning this study with the Lord’s Prayer is beginning with a Teacher and a pattern, not with a man’s own instincts, which run straight to the shopping list. Week One is here to put the words of Jesus in a man’s mouth and let them retrain his heart, so that prayer becomes what it was meant to be: a son lifting his eyes to his Father before he ever lowers them to his needs.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Our Father in Heaven
paras: Two words reframe everything: Our Father. The God a man approaches in prayer is not a reluctant official to be appeased, not a distant force to be flattered, not a judge whose verdict is still pending. He is a Father — and after the gospel, a man knows exactly how he came to call God that. He did not earn the name. His iniquity was laid on the Servant, Christ’s righteousness was credited to him, and on that ground alone he was adopted as a son. So Our Father is not sentimentality; it is gospel. It is the address of a man who has been brought near at infinite cost.

And the word is Our, not only My. Jesus teaches a man to pray as part of a family, not as a religious individualist. Even alone in his room, a man prays Our Father, joining his voice to the whole people of God. This quietly heals the isolation of the dust, where a man feels he is the only one struggling. He is not. He prays with brothers, to a shared Father.

Then: in heaven. The Father is tender, but He is not small. He is in heaven — sovereign, unlimited, able to do far more than a man can ask or think. The two truths have to be held together: Father keeps God from being terrifying; in heaven keeps Him from being trivial. A man who loses the first grovels; a man who loses the second presumes. Held together, they produce the posture of true prayer — a child climbing confidently into the lap of a King.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Hallowed, Kingdom, Will

heads.text: AUGUSTINE — prayer as the exercise of desire

paras: The first petition is not about the man at all: may your name be kept holy. The older English word is hallowed, and it means to treat as holy, to set apart, to honor as supremely precious. The first thing Jesus teaches a man to pray for is that God’s name — His character, His reputation, His glory — would be honored as holy, in the world and first of all in the praying man’s own heart. This is the great reorientation. Before a man asks for anything, he asks that God be treated as God. Luther taught that God’s name is dishonored two ways — by false teaching about Him and by a life that contradicts Him — and the second one starts in the praying man’s own divided heart.

The second petition widens the gaze: Let your Kingdom come. A man asks for the reign of God to advance — in the world, in the church, and in the unsurrendered corners of his own life. To pray it is to pray, in part, let my little kingdom go: the petty domain where the man rules for his own comfort and glory. The prayer trains a man to want God’s rule more than his own control, which is precisely the surrender a dust-clinging soul resists and most needs.

The third petition brings heaven down to earth: Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. In heaven, God’s will is done instantly, joyfully, completely. The man prays for that same glad obedience on earth — and in himself first. This is not grim resignation (“I suppose Your will must be done”); it is glad alignment (“let Your will be done here as gladly as it is done above”). Together, these three petitions perform surgery on a man’s wants. They do not merely ask God for things; they reshape what the man asks for, until his deepest desire is the honoring of the Name, the coming of the Kingdom, and the doing of the Will. A man cannot pray this honestly for long and stay curved in on himself.

Augustine’s letter to Proba answers the objection buried under the Lord’s Prayer: if the Father knows what a man needs before he asks, why the asking? Because prayer was never for God’s information. It is for the man’s enlargement — desire exercised until the vessel can hold what God already intended to pour in. Which explains the order Jesus teaches. Three petitions about God before one word about the man is not divine vanity; it is surgery on desire. Holy name, kingdom, will — a man who prays these honestly finds, over months, that he wants different things than he did. The prayer is reshaping the wanting. Prayer does not inform God of your desires. It rearranges them — until you want what He is already preparing to give. So prayer is the honest speech of a forgiven man — and the first honest thing is that his wants need reordering.

stations.verse: When he finished praying in a certain place, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples.
note: The request is the doorway to this whole study. These were not prayerless men; they were Jews who had prayed since childhood. Yet watching Jesus pray, they realized they did not actually know how. There is great humility and great hope in their request. Humility: a praying man admitting he needs to be taught to pray. Hope: a Teacher who answers by handing him the very words. The man in the dust who feels he does not know how to pray is in the best possible position — the position of the disciples, asking to be taught.
stations.question: Can you pray the disciples’ own prayer this week — “Lord, teach me to pray” — admitting you do not have it figured out, and asking to be taught?
stations.gloss: to pray; built from pros (toward) and euchomai (to pray, to wish). The most common New Testament word for prayer, and always prayer addressed to God. It is simply turning the whole self toward Him in speech.
stations.live: Before you say anything to God tomorrow morning, turn your chair toward the window, open your hands, and say one sentence: Lord, teach me to pray.
body: The disciples watched Jesus proseuchomai and wanted what they saw. The word itself is humble — it does not require eloquence, only a turning toward God. To pray is, at root, to face Him and speak; the learning is in letting Him teach the heart that faces Him. You do not need impressive words to pray. You need to turn toward the Father — and to ask Him to teach you the rest.
The man in the dust who can barely form a sentence to God has already begun: he has turned toward Him and asked to be taught.

stations.verse: Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
note: Everything hangs on the first two words. Jesus could have taught the disciples to begin “Almighty God” or “Sovereign Lord” — both true. Instead He teaches them to begin Our Father. This is the gospel made into an address. A man dares to call the holy God Father only because he has been adopted, and he has been adopted only because his sin was carried by the Son. So the prayer opens with the whole gospel compressed into a relationship: not petitioner to judge, but child to Father. And then immediately, before any request, the first concern — that the Father’s name be kept holy, treated as the holy and precious thing it is.
stations.question: When you pray, do you come as a child to a Father, or as a petitioner to a judge? What would change in your prayers this week if “Our Father” were truly your starting point?
stations.gloss: to hallow, to make or treat as holy, to sanctify, to set apart as sacred. To hallow God’s name is to honor it as utterly distinct, supremely precious, holy above all.
stations.live: Pick one place this week where God’s name is being treated cheaply in your own mouth or home — a habit of speech, a joke, a silence — and change it on purpose.
body: The first petition is hagiazō directed at the Name — a plea that God be treated as holy, in the world and in the praying man’s own heart. It is striking that the first thing a child asks of his Father is not for himself, but that the Father be honored as holy. The healthiest prayer a man can pray begins not ‘help me’ but ‘be honored’ — and a heart that learns that order is being healed.
The man in the dust, curved in on his own needs, is straightened by a prayer that makes him long first for his Father’s name to be kept holy.

stations.verse: Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
note: Two petitions, one direction: God’s reign and God’s will, advancing on earth as they already stand in heaven. To pray Let your Kingdom come is to ask God to extend His rule — and to volunteer one’s own life as territory. To pray Let your will be done is to ask for the same glad, complete obedience on earth that the angels render above. Together they are the great surrender, prayed daily: not my kingdom but Yours, not my will but Yours. This is the prayer that loosens a man’s grip on the little kingdom of self where the dust always gathers.
stations.question: Where is there still a “little kingdom” of your own — a corner of life where you rule for your comfort — that “Let your Kingdom come” is asking you to surrender?
stations.gloss: kingdom, reign, royal rule; not primarily a place but the active exercise of a king’s authority. “Let your Kingdom come” asks for God’s reigning to break in, not for a location on a map.
stations.live: Name the one decision this week you would normally make without asking. Stop before you make it and say out loud, Let your Kingdom come here.
body: Because basileia is reign more than realm, the petition is deeply personal: it asks God to reign here, now, in this man, over this life. To pray it honestly is to invite the King to rule the very places a man has been ruling for himself. To pray ‘Let your Kingdom come’ is, quietly, to pray ‘let my kingdom go’ — and that surrender is the doorway out of the dust.
The man in the dust often clings to a small kingdom of control. This petition gently pries his fingers loose and hands the throne back to God.

stations.verse: For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!
note: Paul shows what makes “Our Father” possible. A man does not call God Father by natural right; he cries Abba by the Spirit of adoption, given to him in the gospel. The cry is the Spirit’s own work in the heart of a forgiven man. Abba is the intimate, trusting word of a child to a beloved father — not formal, not distant, but close. The same Spirit who raised Christ now lives in the believer and teaches him to pray the family name. This is why a man can pray the Lord’s Prayer as more than recitation: the Spirit Himself is forming the cry Our Father in his chest.
stations.question: Do you experience prayer as the Spirit drawing a trusting “Abba, Father” out of you, or as a duty you perform toward a distant God? What might open you to the first?
stations.gloss: the Aramaic word for father, intimate and trusting, the word a child used in the home. Not childish, but childlike — the address of a son secure in his father’s love, not a servant unsure of his standing.
stations.live: Once a day, before the list, say the word Father slowly and wait a breath before you say anything else.
body: That the Spirit teaches believers to cry Abba means prayer is meant to be intimate, not anxious. The forgiven man approaches not as a nervous servant hoping for a hearing, but as a son climbing into a lap, sure of his welcome. The Spirit in you is not coaching you to grovel. He is teaching you to climb into the Father’s lap and say ‘Abba.’
The man in the dust who prays as a frightened servant can let the Spirit retrain his voice into the Abba of a beloved son.

stations.verse: Yahweh is near to all those who call on him, to all who call on him in truth.
note: The whole of prayer rests on this promise: Yahweh is near to all those who call on him. Not near to the eloquent, the worthy, or the spiritually advanced — near to all who call, in truth. The only qualifier is truth: honesty, sincerity, the real self brought to God rather than a performance. This is enormous relief for the man in the dust. He does not have to summon a near God; God is already near to the one who calls. He does not have to polish his words; he has to be truthful. The prayer Jesus teaches is prayed to a God who has already drawn near to hear it.
stations.question: Have you been trying to call on a distant God you must somehow summon, or trusting that Yahweh is already near to all who call on him in truth? What does “in truth” ask of your prayers?
stations.gloss: near, close at hand, present. The same word used for a near kinsman, the relative close enough to act on your behalf. God is qārōb to all who call — not distant and approached only with difficulty, but already close.
stations.live: The next time you feel far from God, speak one true sentence to Him out loud — not a polished one, a true one — and trust that He is already near.
body: Because God is qārōb, prayer is not shouting across a chasm to a far-off deity; it is speaking to One already at hand. The man does not generate God’s nearness by his fervor; he simply speaks, in truth, to a God who is already near. You are not trying to get God’s attention from far away. He is already near — near as a kinsman — to every honest cry.
The man in the dust who feels God is distant can rest in this: Yahweh is near to all who call on him in truth, and the dust does not push Him away.

practices.title: PRAY IT SLOWLY, ONE PHRASE A DAY
practices.body: This week, take just the opening of the prayer — Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy, let your Kingdom come, let your will be done. Pray one phrase a day, slowly, expanding it in your own words. On “Our Father,” dwell on your adoption. On “may your name be kept holy,” ask that God be honored in your home and heart. Luther prayed this way his whole life and said he never exhausted it. Do not rush. Let one phrase fill a day.

practices.title: CATCH THE SHOPPING LIST
practices.body: Notice this week how quickly your prayers default to the list — give me, fix this, help them. Do not scold yourself; just notice. Then, before the list, deliberately pray the first three petitions: may your name be kept holy, let your Kingdom come, let your will be done. Put God first on purpose. Watch how praying for His glory before your needs slowly reorders what you even want.

practices.title: NAME YOUR LITTLE KINGDOM
practices.body: Identify one “little kingdom” — a corner of life you rule for your own comfort or control. Write it down. Then pray “Let your Kingdom come” specifically over it: “Father, let Your reign come here. My kingdom go.” Surrender is rarely a single dramatic act; it is usually a daily prayer. Pray this one daily this week and watch your grip loosen.

practices.title: PRAY IT WITH ANOTHER MAN
practices.body: Find one brother this week — a friend, a son, a man at church — and pray the first half of the Lord’s Prayer out loud together, once, slowly. Our Father, not my Father. Jesus taught a family prayer. Let a second voice remind you that you are not the only one on the ground.

practices.title: HANG YOUR DAY ON THE FIRST WORD
practices.body: Each morning before your feet hit the floor, say two words: Our Father. Nothing else yet. Let the whole day start from the address, before a single need is named. When the day goes wrong at noon, say the two words again.

title: Teach Us to Pray · I
subtitle: the Father, the Name, the Kingdom, the Will
keyVerse: “Lord, teach us to pray” “Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.”

passage.text: When he finished praying in a certain place, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples.”
He said to them, “When you pray, say, ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. May your Kingdom come. May your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven.
Give us day by day our daily bread.
Forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’ ”
Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

stationsIntro: These five passages open up the address and the first petitions of the Lord’s Prayer — the Father a forgiven man comes to, and the God-centered longings the prayer plants in him. Read each slowly. Let the commentary land before you answer. Then sit with the word study beneath it. The thread leads back to the dust — and to the Father who teaches a son to pray.
lifeIntro: This week is about letting the first half of the Lord’s Prayer retrain your heart — to come as a son, and to long for God’s name, kingdom, and will before your own needs. The goal is not to recite the prayer but to be remade by it. Five practices for the next seven days.
prayer: Our Father in heaven, I come to You as a son, not because I earned the name but because Your Son carried my sin and gave me His place. May Your name be kept holy — in the world, in my house, in my mouth. Let Your Kingdom come into the corners I have been running for myself. Let Your will be done in me as gladly as it is done in heaven. I do not know how to pray as I ought. Teach me, the way You taught the men who asked. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Our Father in heaven, I come to You as a son, not because I earned the name but because Your Son carried my sin and gave me His place.
May Your name be kept holy — in the world, in my house, in my mouth.
Let Your Kingdom come into the corners I have been running for myself.
Let Your will be done in me as gladly as it is done in heaven.
I do not know how to pray as I ought.
Teach me, the way You taught the men who asked.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Jesus answers the request to be taught with a prayer, and the prayer starts with God, not with you. You come as an adopted son to a Father who is tender and sovereign at once. His name, His Kingdom, His will come first — and that order is how He heals a heart that has been curved in on itself.
benediction: Jesus teaches you to begin not with your needs but with Himself. Our Father in heaven — tender and sovereign, near and exalted. May your name be kept holy — let Yourself be honored as holy, in the world and in me. Let your Kingdom come — let Your reign break into every corner I have been ruling for myself. Let your will be done — let me obey You here as gladly as You are obeyed above. Three petitions about God before a single word about yourself. This is not God demanding to be flattered. It is a Father healing a self-obsessed soul by lifting its eyes off itself.

So this week, when you pray, lift up your eyes — first, before anything, to the Father. When the shopping list rises, lift your eyes above it to the hallowing of His name. When you feel the dust of self-rule, lift your eyes and pray His kingdom into the corner you have been guarding. When your will and His seem far apart, lift your eyes to heaven, where His will is done with joy, and ask for that joy on earth, in you.

You do not have to be eloquent. Yahweh is near to all those who call on him. You do not have to summon a distant God; the Spirit of adoption is already in you, drawing the cry Abba, Father out of your chest. Come as a son. Begin with the Father. Let the first half of the prayer reorder your heart this week — and next week the prayer turns to the rest.
carry: What would change this week if the first thing you wanted, every morning, was for your Father’s name to be kept holy?

pulls: Bread for the body, pardon for the soul, deliverance from the evil one. In three short petitions, Jesus teaches a man to bring his entire life to a Father who cares about all of it.
paras: Last week the Lord’s Prayer lifted a man’s eyes to his Father and to God’s name, kingdom, and will. Only now, after the great reorientation, does the prayer turn to the man’s own needs — and when it does, it covers the whole of human need in three short petitions. Give us today our daily bread. Forgive us our debts. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. Provision, pardon, and protection. Body, soul, and the danger no one sees coming. Past sin forgiven, present need supplied, future danger guarded. The man’s entire life, lifted up to the Father in three short requests.

Notice the order, because it preaches. The prayer does not begin with the man’s needs, but it does not ignore them either. After God is honored first, the man is invited to bring everything — his stomach, his guilt, his weakness — to a Father who cares about all of it. The God who is honored as holy in heaven is also the God who feeds His children’s bodies and forgives their debts and guards them from the evil one. Greatness and tenderness in the same Father, addressed in the same prayer.

And notice what is missing from these petitions: any hint of the man’s worthiness. He asks for bread he has not earned, forgiveness he cannot deserve, and deliverance he cannot accomplish. The entire second half of the prayer is the posture of the gospel — an empty-handed son receiving from a generous Father. The man who walked the gospel prays this naturally now: he already knows he brings nothing and receives everything. This week sits with these three petitions and teaches a man to bring his whole real life — dust and all — to the Father who delights to give.

sections.heading: WHAT WE ARE GOING AFTER
paras: This week goes after the freedom of bringing real, ordinary, embarrassing need to God — and the particular weight of the petition most men rush past: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. The prayer ties a man’s receiving of forgiveness to his extending of it, not because his forgiving earns God’s pardon (the gospel killed that idea), but because a man who has truly received mercy cannot hoard it. An unforgiving heart is a sign that the gospel has not yet landed. The petition exposes it and the prayer begins to heal it.

The goal this week is to learn to pray for daily bread without shame, for forgiveness without despair, and for deliverance without bravado. Daily bread teaches dependence — a man who asks for today’s provision today cannot stockpile his way to self-sufficiency. Forgive us our debts teaches ongoing humility — even a justified man still prays for pardon, not to be re-justified but to keep the relationship clear. And deliver us from the evil one teaches honest weakness — a man admitting he cannot stand against temptation and the evil one in his own strength. Three petitions, three deaths to self-reliance, three doorways out of the dust.

sections.heading: WHY START HERE
paras: Because a forgiven man can drift into two opposite errors: praying only lofty spiritual prayers while hiding his ordinary needs, or praying only anxious need-prayers while forgetting he is a beloved son. The second half of the Lord’s Prayer corrects both. It dignifies the request for bread and it keeps the request for forgiveness central. Week Two is here to teach a man to bring his whole self — body and soul, past and future, provision and pardon and protection — to the Father, holding nothing back as too small and nothing back as too shameful.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Daily Bread and Forgiven Debts
paras: Give us today our daily bread. It is a startling thing for the Son of God to put in a man’s mouth — a prayer about food. But that is the point: the Father cares about the body, the budget, the ordinary needs a man is half-ashamed to pray about. And the word daily teaches a rhythm of dependence. The prayer does not ask for a year’s supply or a guarantee of security; it asks for today’s bread, today — the way Israel gathered manna one morning at a time and could not hoard it. A man who prays this honestly is learning to live in daily reliance on a Father who provides, rather than in the anxious self-sufficiency that never feels safe enough.

Then the prayer turns to the deeper hunger: Forgive us our debts. Even here — even after the gospel, even for a man already justified — Jesus teaches daily prayer for forgiveness. This is not a contradiction of justification. A man’s standing as a son is settled forever; but the relationship still gets clouded by daily sin, and the prayer keeps it clear, the way a son who is permanently a son still says “I’m sorry” to keep the air clean between him and his father. The justified man does not pray for forgiveness to be re-saved. He prays it to walk in unbroken fellowship with the Father who already forgave him completely at the cross.

And the petition carries a hook a man cannot wriggle off: as we also forgive our debtors. Jesus is not making God’s forgiveness a wage paid for a man’s forgiving. He is saying that a heart truly gripped by mercy becomes merciful, and a heart that refuses to forgive reveals it has not yet felt its own forgiveness. The unforgiving servant of Jesus’ parable was forgiven a fortune and then throttled a man over pennies — and his refusal exposed that the mercy had never reached his heart. To pray this petition honestly, a man must hold his own grudges up to the cross and let them go.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Lead Us Not, Deliver Us
paras: The final petition turns to the danger a man cannot face alone: Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. The phrasing has puzzled readers — God tempts no one, James says plainly. The sense is a humble plea: do not let me be led into the testing that would undo me; spare me the trial I am too weak to bear, and where trial comes, do not let me fall. It is the prayer of a man who has stopped trusting his own strength against sin — who knows, after the gospel, that he is not as strong as he pretends and the enemy is not as small as he hopes.

Deliver us from the evil one. The Christian life is not merely self-improvement against bad habits; it is rescue from a real and personal enemy who prowls. The petition admits a man cannot deliver himself. He does not ask for strength to outlast the enemy; he asks the Father to deliver him out of reach. This is the same posture as the whole gospel: not “give me the power to save myself” but “rescue me, for I cannot.” The man in the dust who has been white-knuckling his way against temptation is taught here to pray for deliverance instead of relying on willpower.

And so the prayer that began with the Father ends in the Father’s hands — provision, pardon, protection, all received from above. The closing line many manuscripts carry — For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever — returns the prayer to where it started: God’s glory, God’s reign, God’s power. The whole prayer is a circle that begins and ends in God, with the man’s needs held safely in the middle. To pray it through is to be carried from God’s glory, down into one’s real and humbling needs, and back up to God’s glory again. A man cannot pray it daily and stay either proud or despairing. It will not let him.

When Luther’s barber, Peter Beskendorf, asked him how to pray, Luther sent back a method: take a text and wind four strands out of it — instruction, thanksgiving, confession, petition. In that same letter he walks through the Lord’s Prayer petition by petition, putting each one into his own words before he ever turns to the garland. The second half of the prayer is the four strands in miniature. Daily bread teaches dependence and prompts thanks. Forgive us our debts is confession. Bring us not into temptation is petition. A man who works this half of the prayer slowly has all four strands available every morning without ever having to generate material of his own. You are not required to produce something to pray. You are required to work a text — which is why a man with a Bible open rarely runs out of things to say to God. So prayer is the honest speech of a forgiven man — and the words were handed to him so he would not have to invent them.

stations.verse: Give us today our daily bread.
note: One plain sentence, and it dignifies every ordinary need a man is tempted to think too small for God. The Father who is honored as holy in heaven wants to be asked for bread. And the word daily resets a man’s whole relationship to provision: not a stockpile that lets him stop depending, but today’s bread today, received from an open hand. This is the cure for the anxious self-sufficiency that drives a man to secure his own future and never feel secure. He is taught to ask, and to trust, one day at a time.
stations.question: What ordinary, “too small for God” need have you been carrying alone instead of asking your Father for — and what would change if you brought it to Him today?
stations.gloss: usually rendered “daily.” In the New Testament it appears only in this petition (Matthew 6:11; Luke 11:3). Its derivation is debated: it may mean “for the coming day” or “needed for existence.” Either way it points to provision measured one day at a time.
stations.live: Tonight, name tomorrow’s one ordinary need out loud to God — the bill, the meeting, the tired body — and ask for it by name.
body: The strangeness of epiousios is the lesson: the prayer asks not for abundance or security but for enough, today. It trains a man out of the hoarding instinct and into daily trust — the manna rhythm, where yesterday’s supply will not keep and tomorrow’s is not yet given. God gives bread for today, not a stockpile that would let you stop needing Him — because He wants the son, not just the son’s independence.
The man in the dust who is exhausted from securing his own future is invited to ask only for today’s bread, and to trust the Father for tomorrow when it comes.

stations.verse: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
note: A justified man still prays this — and that is not a contradiction. His standing is settled; his daily fellowship still needs the clearing that confession brings, the way a beloved son still says sorry to his father. But the petition’s sting is in the second clause: as we also forgive our debtors. Jesus binds the receiving of mercy to the giving of it — not as payment, but as evidence. A man who has truly felt the weight of his own forgiven debt cannot clutch a grudge against another. If he can, the mercy has not yet reached his heart.
stations.question: Is there a debtor you have refused to forgive — and what does that refusal reveal about how deeply your own forgiveness has landed?
stations.gloss: a debt, something owed; here, sin pictured as a debt owed to God. The image is financial: sin runs up a debt the man cannot pay, and forgiveness is the cancellation of what is owed.
stations.live: Write the name of one person who owes you on a slip of paper. Carry it all week, and each time you touch it, pray, Forgive me as I forgive him.
body: If sin is opheilēma — a debt — then the man who grasps the size of his own cancelled debt is undone by it, and cannot then choke a fellow servant over a smaller one. The petition assumes a man who has felt the cancellation. Forgiving others is the overflow of being forgiven much. The measure of how deeply you have felt your own forgiveness is how freely you forgive the one who owes you.
The man in the dust nursing a grudge is invited to set his grievance beside the debt the cross cancelled for him — and let it go.

stations.verse: Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’
note: This is the prayer of a man who has stopped overestimating himself. He does not ask for stronger willpower; he asks not to be led into the testing that would break him, and to be delivered from the evil one when the testing comes. It is deep humility: an admission that he cannot stand in his own strength against sin and the enemy. After the gospel, a man prays this honestly — he knows he is not strong, that deliverance must come from outside him, that the same grace that saved him must also keep him.
stations.question: Where have you been relying on willpower to resist temptation instead of praying for deliverance — and what testing do you most need to ask God to spare you from this week?
stations.gloss: to draw to oneself, and so to rescue, to deliver. It is the word Paul uses in Who will deliver me out of the body of this death? A word of rescue, not reinforcement. The man asks to be hauled out, not handed better equipment.
stations.live: Name the one temptation that finds you at the same hour every week. At that hour this week, stop and pray three words before anything else: Father, deliver me.
body: That the petition uses rhuomai means the goal is rescue, not self-improvement. The man does not pray “make me strong enough to win” but “deliver me” — the cry of one who knows evil is escaped by being rescued, not by being tough. The most honest prayer against temptation is not ‘I’ve got this’ but ‘deliver me’ — the cry of a man done trusting his own strength.
The man in the dust who keeps losing to the same sin can stop white-knuckling and start praying for deliverance from the One strong enough to give it.

stations.verse: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
note: Paul gives the everyday shape of the Lord’s Prayer’s second half: bring everything to God. Not the spiritual things only — in everything, by prayer. The cure for anxiety is not suppressing the worry but transferring it, request by request, to the Father, with thanksgiving. And the promise is not always the thing asked for, but a peace that guards the heart, a peace beyond understanding. The man who learns to pray his daily bread and his real fears finds the worry replaced not by answers but by a guarding peace.
stations.question: What anxiety have you been carrying instead of converting into a request to God — and would you be willing, this week, to hand it over with thanksgiving?
stations.gloss: to guard, to keep watch over; from phrouros, a guard or watchman. It is the word for a sentry keeping a city. God’s peace phroureō — keeps watch over — the heart of the man who brings everything to Him.
stations.live: Take the thing you worried about last night and turn it into a single sentence of request, then add one sentence of thanks. Do it before breakfast.
body: The image is a garrison: when a man transfers his requests to God, peace posts a guard around his heart and mind. He does not have to defend his own peace by solving everything; the peace of God stands sentry over him while he trusts. When you hand your worries to the Father, His peace mounts a guard around your heart that your circumstances cannot break through.
The man in the dust, pressed on every side by anxiety, finds that prayer does not always change the situation — but it posts a divine guard over his soul in the middle of it.

stations.verse: Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and may find grace for help in time of need.
note: This is the confidence that makes the whole prayer possible. The forgiven man approaches not a throne of judgment but a throne of grace — and he comes with boldness, confidence, freedom of speech, because his High Priest has already secured his welcome. He comes to receive mercy for his failures and grace for his needs, in the very moment of need. This is the gospel feeding prayer: a man dares to ask for bread, pardon, and deliverance because the throne he approaches is a throne of grace, and the One who sits on it has already laid his iniquity on the Servant.
stations.question: Do you draw near to God in prayer with boldness or with hesitation — and how does knowing it is a “throne of grace” change the way you would come this week?
stations.gloss: confidence, boldness, freedom of speech; the freedom of a citizen to speak openly, or a child to speak freely to a father without fear. The opposite of the cowering of a guilty servant.
stations.live: This week, when you catch yourself approaching God with an apology for existing, stop and start again with Father, instead.
body: The forgiven man comes to the throne with parrēsia — not the nervous approach of one unsure of his welcome, but the bold, open speech of a son who knows he belongs. The gospel turns the throne of judgment into a throne of grace a man can approach freely. You may speak to God with the open boldness of a welcomed son — because the cross already settled whether you belong at the throne.
The man in the dust who approaches God timidly, unsure of his welcome, is invited to come with the parrēsia the gospel bought him — boldly, to a throne of grace.

practices.title: PRAY YOUR REAL BREAD
practices.body: Each day this week, name one specific, ordinary need — a bill, a meal, an energy you lack, a problem at work — and pray “Give me today my daily bread” over exactly that. Resist the urge to keep prayer “spiritual.” The Father wants to be asked for bread. Practice bringing the ordinary to Him until no need feels too small to pray.

practices.title: FORGIVE ONE DEBTOR
practices.body: Identify one person who owes you — an apology, a debt, a wrong unmade-right. This week, hold their debt up beside the debt the cross cancelled for you, and pray “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” over that specific person. Forgiveness is rarely a feeling first; it is usually a decision prayed repeatedly until the heart catches up. Begin the decision this week.

practices.title: TRADE WILLPOWER FOR ‘DELIVER ME’
practices.body: Pick the temptation you most often fight by gritting your teeth. This week, the moment you feel it, stop relying on willpower and pray instead: “Bring me not into this; deliver me from the evil one.” Ask the Father to rescue you rather than trying to out-muscle the sin. Notice the difference between white-knuckling and crying for deliverance — and which one a forgiven son was meant to do.

practices.title: KEEP A BREAD LIST
practices.body: Keep a short list this week of the ordinary things you asked for and what came. Food on the table. A conversation that went better than it should have. A day you did not have strength for and got through. At the end of the week, read the list back to God as thanks.

practices.title: CONFESS SOMETHING SMALL DAILY
practices.body: Each night this week, before you sleep, name one specific thing from that day that you need forgiven. Not a category. The thing. Then pray, Forgive us our debts, and go to sleep a son whose account is clear.

title: Teach Us to Pray · II
subtitle: the bread, the debts, the deliverance
keyVerse: Give us today our daily bread. Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.

passage.text: Give us today our daily bread.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’
Give us day by day our daily bread.
Forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’ ”

stationsIntro: These five passages open up the second half of the Lord’s Prayer — the provision, pardon, and protection a forgiven man brings to his Father. Read each slowly. Let the commentary land before you answer. Then sit with the word study beneath it. The thread leads back to the dust — and to the Father who feeds, forgives, and delivers His sons.
lifeIntro: This week is about learning to bring your whole real life to the Father through the second half of the Lord’s Prayer — your provision, your pardon, your protection. The goal is honest, dependent, daily prayer. Five practices for the next seven days.
prayer: Father, give me today my daily bread — not a stockpile, just today’s. Forgive me my debts; You know every one of them, and You paid them at the cross. Make me a man who forgives what is owed to me, because I have been forgiven more. Bring me not into temptation. Deliver me from the evil one. I am not as strong as I pretend. I come to the throne of grace with boldness only because Your Son opened the way. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, give me today my daily bread — not a stockpile, just today’s.
Forgive me my debts; You know every one of them, and You paid them at the cross.
Make me a man who forgives what is owed to me, because I have been forgiven more.
Bring me not into temptation. Deliver me from the evil one.
I am not as strong as I pretend.
I come to the throne of grace with boldness only because Your Son opened the way.
Amen.
bottomLine: The second half of the Lord’s Prayer brings your whole life to the Father: bread for the body, pardon for the soul, rescue from the evil one. You ask for all three empty-handed, because that is how the gospel taught you to come. A man who has felt his own debt cancelled cannot keep clutching the debts of others.
benediction: See how the whole prayer keeps the gospel at its center. You ask for bread you did not earn, forgiveness you cannot deserve, and deliverance you cannot accomplish — the empty-handed posture of a son who learned in the gospel that he brings nothing and receives everything. Even the petition that stings, forgive us as we also forgive, is not the gospel undone but the gospel overflowing: a man who has felt the size of his cancelled debt cannot keep clutching the small debts others owe him. The mercy that saved him makes him merciful, or it has not yet reached his heart.

So this week, when an ordinary need feels too small to mention, lift up your eyes and ask for your daily bread. When yesterday’s sin clouds today’s fellowship, lift your eyes to the throne of grace and confess, not to be re-saved but to walk clear with your Father. When a grudge tightens in your chest, lift your eyes to the debt the cross cancelled and let your debtor go. When temptation comes and your willpower fails, lift your eyes and cry “deliver me” instead of “I’ve got this.”

You may come with boldness, because it is the throne of grace, and your welcome was secured by the Servant’s wounds, not your performance. The prayer that begins with the Father ends in the Father’s hands, and your needs are held safely in the middle. Pray it through this week — from His glory, down into your real and humbling needs, and back up to His glory again — and let it carry you, daily, out of the dust.
carry: What have you been carrying alone this week that your Father has been waiting for you to ask Him for?

pulls: Paul rarely prays for better circumstances. He prays that the eyes of the heart would open — so a man would finally see what the gospel has already made true of him.
paras: The Lord handed you the pattern of prayer in His own words. Now the school moves to the apostle Paul, who prayed that pattern into specific, soaring requests for the people he loved — and whose prayers, recorded in his letters, show a forgiven man exactly what to ask for. Most men, when they pray for others, pray almost entirely about circumstances: heal this, fix that, change the situation. Paul prays for circumstances too, but it is striking how rarely. What he prays for, again and again, is that people would know — that the eyes of their hearts would be opened to see what is already true of them in Christ.

Listen to what Paul actually asks for the Ephesians. Not better circumstances. Not relief from suffering. He asks that God would give them a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, with the eyes of your hearts enlightened, so that they would know three things: the hope of his calling, the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, and the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe. Paul’s deepest prayer for them is that they would see — really see — what the gospel has already made true.

This is a revolution in how a man prays, for himself and for others. The man in the dust does not usually need new facts; he needs the facts he already has to move from his head to his heart, from information to sight. He knows, in theory, that he is forgiven, adopted, an heir. But he does not see it; it does not grip him; the dust feels more real than the inheritance. Paul’s prayer is the cure: a plea that God would open the eyes of the heart so that what is already true would finally be seen. This week teaches a man to pray Paul’s prayer — for himself and for the men he loves.

sections.heading: WHAT WE ARE GOING AFTER
paras: This week goes after a change in the content of a man’s prayers — from a list of circumstances to be fixed toward a plea for eyes to be opened. Paul models a kind of intercession most men have never tried: praying that someone would know the hope of his calling, see the riches of his inheritance, and feel the power that raised Christ now at work in him. These are not requests for things to be added to a person’s life; they are requests for sight — that a person would perceive the riches that are already his in Christ but lie unseen, like a fortune in an account a man has forgotten he owns.

The goal this week is to let Paul retrain your asking. When you pray for yourself in the dust, learn to pray less “change my situation” and more “open my eyes to what is already true.” When you pray for others, learn to pray less “fix their circumstances” and more “let them see their hope, their inheritance, Your power.” This does not mean you stop praying about real troubles — Paul did not. It means you learn that the deepest need, under every trouble, is to see Christ and what He has secured — because a man who sees that can endure almost any circumstance, and a man who does not see it is poor in the middle of riches.

sections.heading: WHY START HERE
paras: Because a forgiven man who has learned the pattern of the Lord’s Prayer now needs to learn its content stretched to its full reach — and Paul’s prayers are the inspired model. The man in the dust has the gospel in his head and cannot feel it in his chest, and no amount of new information will close that gap; only the Spirit opening the eyes of the heart will. Week Three is here to teach a man to pray for sight — his own and others’ — so that the inheritance he already owns stops being a doctrine he believes and becomes a reality he sees.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Eyes of the Heart
paras: Paul prays that God would give the Ephesians a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened. Notice the organ: the eyes of the heart. Paul is not praying for more information in their heads; they already had sound teaching. He is praying for sight in their hearts — the capacity to perceive spiritual reality as real, to have truth land with the weight of seeing rather than merely the assent of believing. There is a vast difference between knowing the sun is warm and feeling it on your face. Paul prays for the second.

This is the answer to a frustration the man in the dust knows well. He believes the gospel is true. He can recite that he is forgiven and adopted. And yet it does not move him; it sits inert; the dust feels weightier than the promise. The problem is not a lack of facts but a lack of sight — the eyes of the heart are dim. And Paul’s response is not to pile on more facts but to pray. Enlightened eyes are a gift of the Spirit, asked for in prayer, not achieved by study. A man cannot manufacture sight; he can only ask the One who gives it.

So the first thing this prayer teaches is a humbling and liberating truth: the movement of the gospel from head to heart is God’s work, requested in prayer. The man in the dust who has been straining to feel what he believes can stop straining and start asking. “Father, give me the Spirit of wisdom and revelation. Enlighten the eyes of my heart. Let me see what I already know.” This is a prayer God delights to answer, because it asks for exactly what He longs to give — sight of His Son and His riches.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Three Things to See
paras: Paul names three specific things he wants their opened eyes to see, and they are worth praying for by name. First, the hope of his calling — the certain future the gospel guarantees, the glory ahead that makes present suffering bearable. A man crushed by his circumstances is usually a man who has lost sight of his hope; Paul prays the hope back into view. To see the hope of the calling is to feel the weight of glory pressing back against the weight of the dust.

Second, the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints. Paul wants a staggering thought seen: the inheritance may be not only what the believer gets from God but what God has in His people — His inheritance, as the phrase reads, in the saints. God counts His people as His treasured possession. The man in the dust who feels worthless is praying to see that he is, astonishingly, part of what God Himself treasures. To see that is to have the bottom drop out of one’s sense of insignificance.

Third, the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe — and Paul measures it by the resurrection. The same power that raised Christ from the dead and seated Him above every rule and authority is the power now at work toward the believer. This is not a trickle of help; it is resurrection power, the greatest force in the universe, aimed at the man who believes. The man in the dust who feels too weak to change is praying to see that the power working in him is the power that emptied the tomb. Three things to see: a certain hope, a treasured belonging, an unstoppable power. Paul prays they would be seen — and a man should pray the same, for himself and for every man he loves.

Keller’s definition has two halves and both are load-bearing: prayer is conversation, which keeps it ordinary and verbal and tied to what God has said, and prayer is encounter, which keeps it from degenerating into a task list. Keep the first alone and prayer flattens. Keep the second alone and it evaporates. Ephesians 1 is Paul praying for the second half. He does not ask that the Ephesians learn more facts; he asks that the eyes of their hearts be enlightened — that what they already know would become something they see. The distinction between knowing about God and knowing God is the whole burden of this prayer. A man can hold every doctrine in this letter and still have never once met the God the doctrines are about. So prayer is the honest speech of a forgiven man — and it is aimed at a Person, not an outcome.

stations.verse: that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him,
note: Paul’s first request is for wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of God — a deeper, experiential knowing of God Himself. Not knowledge about God added to a file, but knowledge of God that grips and warms. And notice it is asked for: this kind of knowing is a gift of the Spirit, prayed for, not an achievement earned by effort. The man who wants to know God more deeply does not first need a better study method; he needs to ask the Father of glory for the Spirit who reveals.
stations.question: Do you long to know God more deeply, or only to know more facts about Him — and have you ever simply asked Him for the Spirit of wisdom and revelation?
stations.gloss: knowledge, recognition; built on epi-and gnōsis. Paul uses it for knowing God and His will (Colossians 1:9–10), not for collecting information. Not acquaintance with facts but the knowledge of a Person.
stations.live: Choose one truth you already believe about God and pray it back to Him every morning this week, asking to know Him, not just the fact.
body: Paul prays for epignōsis of God — the difference between knowing about a man and knowing him. The gospel gives a man facts about God; this prayer asks that the facts become intimate, felt, personal knowledge of God Himself. You can know every true fact about God and still not know Him — and the second is what Paul prays you would receive.
The man in the dust who knows the doctrine but feels distant from God is praying for exactly this: not more facts, but the deep knowing the Spirit gives.

stations.verse: having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints,
note: This is the central petition: enlightened eyes of the heart, so that a man may know his hope and his inheritance. Both are already his — the calling is sure, the inheritance is secured — but they must be seen to do a man any good. A fortune unseen funds nothing. Paul prays that the believer would perceive what he already possesses, so the hope would steady him and the inheritance would dignify him. This is the prayer for the man whose head is full of gospel and whose heart is full of dust: Father, let him see.
stations.question: Which do you most need your eyes opened to see right now — the hope of your calling, or the riches of the inheritance you already have in Christ? Why that one?
stations.gloss: to enlighten, to illuminate, to bring to light, to give light to. The eyes of the heart are phōtizō — flooded with light — so that what was there in the dark becomes visible.
stations.live: Write down one thing already true of you in Christ — forgiven, adopted, heir — and read it aloud at the moment of the day when it feels least true.
body: The image is a dark room full of treasure: nothing is added, but light is switched on, and suddenly the riches already present can be seen. Phōtizō is what a man in the dust needs — not more treasure, but light to see the treasure he already owns in Christ. The inheritance does not need to grow. The lights need to come on — and that is what Paul is praying for you.
The man in the dust is often a rich man sitting in the dark. The prayer is not for more wealth but for the light to see it.

stations.verse: and what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to that working of the strength of his might which he worked in Christ, when he raised him from the dead and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places,
note: Paul saves the most staggering request for last: that they would see the exceeding greatness of his power toward them — and he measures that power by the resurrection. The force now at work toward the believer is the very force that raised Christ from the dead and seated Him above all. This is the answer to the man who feels too weak to change, too far gone, too stuck in the dust. The power aimed at him is not motivational energy; it is resurrection power, the strongest force in existence, and it is directed toward him because he believes.
stations.question: Where do you feel too weak to change — and can you believe that the power at work toward you is the same power that raised Christ from the dead?
stations.gloss: power, might, strength, ability. In these two verses Paul stacks word upon word — greatness, power, working, strength, might — straining language to describe the power directed toward believers.
stations.live: Name one sin or weakness you have given up on changing. Pray over it once a day this week: the power that raised Jesus is aimed at this.
body: The dunamis toward the believer is defined by the resurrection: it is the power that raised the dead Christ. So the strength available to the man in the dust is not a coping mechanism but the same omnipotent force that emptied the tomb, now aimed at him. The power working toward you is not a trickle of help. It is the very might that raised Jesus from the grave.
The man in the dust who feels powerless to rise is praying to see that resurrection power itself is at work toward him.

stations.verse: Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, salutes you, always striving for you in his prayers, that you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.
note: Paul commends Epaphras, who labored in prayer for the Colossians — and notice what he prayed: not for their comfort or ease, but that they would stand perfect and complete in all the will of God. Here again is the Pauline pattern, embodied in another man: intercession aimed not at circumstances but at the inner person — maturity, completeness, standing. And notice the verb: he strove, wrestled, agonized in prayer. This kind of praying for others is labor, not a sentence tacked onto a meal. It is one of the great works a man can do for the brothers he loves.
stations.question: Whom could you strive for in prayer this week — not for his circumstances, but that he would stand complete in Christ?
stations.gloss: to strive, to struggle, to contend as in an athletic contest; the root of “agonize.” Epaphras did not merely mention the Colossians; he labored, strove, wrestled for them in prayer.
stations.live: Pick one brother and set a daily alarm this week. When it goes off, pray one sentence for his inner life, not his circumstances.
body: That intercession is agōnizomai means real prayer for others is effort, not afterthought. Epaphras spent himself in prayer for people he loved, contending for their maturity. This is the dignity and the cost of praying for the brothers. The most loving work you can do for a brother may be the prayer you wrestle through for him when he never knows.
The man in the dust who feels useless to help others is shown a labor he can always perform: to wrestle in prayer for them.

stations.verse: Elisha prayed, and said, “Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.” Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.
note: Elisha’s servant panicked at the surrounding enemy army, seeing only the threat. Elisha did not pray for the army to leave; he prayed for the servant’s eyes to open — and when they did, the servant saw the mountain full of the horses and chariots of fire that had been there all along. The reality had not changed; his sight had. This is a picture of Paul’s whole prayer. The man in the dust, surrounded by what frightens him, most needs not a change of circumstance but opened eyes to see the greater reality already present: God’s presence, power, and protection, more real than the threat.
stations.question: What threat are you seeing so clearly that it has blinded you to the greater reality of God’s presence and power around you — and will you pray Elisha’s prayer: “Open my eyes that I may see”?
stations.gloss: to open the eyes, to open wide, to give sight. Used almost exclusively of opening eyes — physical or spiritual. Elisha prays pāqach over his servant, and the unseen reality becomes visible.
stations.live: The next time fear fills your vision, stop and pray Elisha’s six words — open my eyes, that I may see — before you decide anything.
body: The miracle was not new chariots; it was pāqach — opened eyes to see the chariots already there. So the deepest answer to fear is often not a changed situation but opened sight, perceiving the God who was present all along. The chariots of fire were always there. The servant just could not see them until God opened his eyes — and so it is with you.
The man in the dust surrounded by fears is praying for pāqach — eyes opened to the God whose protection encircles him unseen.

practices.title: PRAY EPHESIANS 1 OVER YOURSELF
practices.body: Each day this week, pray Paul’s prayer over your own name: “Father, give me the Spirit of wisdom and revelation. Open the eyes of my heart. Let me see the hope of my calling, the riches of my inheritance, the power at work toward me.” You are not asking for new facts; you are asking to see the ones you have. Pray it until something shifts from your head to your chest.

practices.title: PRAY FOR ONE MAN’S EYES
practices.body: Choose one brother and, instead of praying about his circumstances, wrestle in prayer this week that the eyes of his heart would be opened — that he would see his hope, his belonging, God’s power toward him. Pray it more than once. You may never tell him. This is the labor of love Epaphras modeled: contending in prayer for another man’s sight.

practices.title: PRAY ELISHA’S PRAYER OVER A FEAR
practices.body: Name one threat that has been filling your vision — a fear so vivid it has crowded out God. This week, when it rises, pray Elisha’s prayer: “Open my eyes that I may see.” Ask not for the threat to vanish but for sight of the greater reality — the chariots of fire, the God already present and strong around you. Practice seeing past the threat to the One who surrounds it.

practices.title: ASK TO SEE, NOT JUST TO KNOW
practices.body: Choose one thing you believe but do not feel — that you are forgiven, that you belong to God, that His power is at work in you. Each day this week, ask God specifically to let you see it, not just affirm it. Then watch for it. Write down the one moment it landed.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER WHAT YOU ASKED FOR HIM
practices.body: By the end of the week, tell the man you have been praying for what you asked — not about his job or his health, but for his eyes to be opened. Say it plainly. Let him know someone is on his knees for his inner life.

title: That You May Know
subtitle: Paul’s prayer that the eyes of the heart would see
keyVerse: that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know

passage.text: For this cause I also, having heard of the faith in the Lord Jesus which is among you, and the love which you have toward all the saints,
don’t cease to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers,
that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him,
having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints,
and what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to that working of the strength of his might
which he worked in Christ, when he raised him from the dead and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places,
far above all rule, authority, power, dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in that which is to come.
He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly,
which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.

stationsIntro: These five passages open up Paul’s prayer that the eyes of the heart would see — the hope, the inheritance, the power already true in Christ. Read each slowly. Let the commentary land before you answer. Then sit with the word study beneath it. The thread leads back to the dust — and to the God who opens blind eyes to see what He has already given.
lifeIntro: This week is about letting Paul retrain the content of your prayers — from fixing circumstances to opening eyes, for yourself and for others. The goal is to learn to pray for sight of what the gospel has already made true. Five practices for the next seven days.
prayer: Father of glory, I know more about You than I have ever seen of You. Give me wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of You. Open the eyes of my heart. Let me see the hope of Your calling, the riches of Your inheritance, and the power that raised Jesus from the dead. Open the eyes of the men I love, too. I cannot make myself see. You can. Please do. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father of glory, I know more about You than I have ever seen of You.
Give me wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of You.
Open the eyes of my heart.
Let me see the hope of Your calling, the riches of Your inheritance, and the power that raised Jesus from the dead.
Open the eyes of the men I love, too.
I cannot make myself see. You can. Please do.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul rarely prays for better circumstances. He prays for sight — that believers would see the hope, the inheritance, and the resurrection power already theirs in Christ. You are not short of riches. You are short of light, and light is what God gives when you ask.
benediction: Paul’s prayer is the prayer your soul most needs, and it is a prayer God delights to answer. You do not need a new gospel; you need light to see the one you have. So Paul prays for wisdom and revelation, for enlightened eyes, for sight of three things you already possess: a hope that steadies you, an inheritance that dignifies you, and a power — resurrection power, the force that emptied the tomb — now at work toward you because you believe. None of it needs to be added. All of it needs to be seen.

So this week, when the dust feels more real than the promise, lift up your eyes — and ask for eyes to lift. Pray Paul’s prayer over yourself: open the eyes of my heart, that I may see. When a brother is crushed, lift your eyes from his circumstances and wrestle in prayer that his eyes would open. When fear fills your vision, pray Elisha’s prayer over it: open my eyes that I may see the chariots of fire that were always there.

The treasure is real and it is yours; you are only sitting in the dark. And the God who is the Father of glory loves to switch on the light. You cannot manufacture sight by straining harder to feel what you believe. But you can ask. And the same Spirit who raised Christ will open the eyes of your heart, in His time, until the inheritance you have believed becomes the inheritance you can see — and a man who sees his riches no longer clings to the dust.
carry: If God opened your eyes this week to one thing already true of you in Christ, which one would you most want to see?

pulls: Paul does not pray that they would know God’s will so they could feel informed. He prays they would be filled with it so they could walk worthy. Sight is for walking. Knowing is for living.
paras: Last week Paul prayed that the eyes of the heart would be opened to see. This week sits with a companion prayer — his prayer for the Colossians — and it shows what opened eyes are for. Paul does not pray that they would know God’s will so they could feel informed. He prays that they would be filled with the knowledge of his will so that they would walk worthily of the Lord. Sight is for walking. Knowing is for living. The prayer moves from the inner eyes opening to the whole life bearing fruit.

And notice how Paul prays — he says since the day we heard this, don’t cease praying. This is persistent, ongoing, refusing-to-quit prayer for people he had never even met in person. It teaches a man that real intercession is not a one-time mention but a steady, unceasing labor. Paul carried these believers before God continually, asking not that their circumstances would ease but that their lives would be filled, fruitful, strengthened, and thankful. It is a staggering prayer to pray for another man, and a more staggering one to have prayed over yourself.

Read what Paul actually asks. To be filled with the knowledge of God’s will. To walk worthily of the Lord, pleasing Him in all respects. To bear fruit in every good work. To grow in the knowledge of God. To be strengthened with all power for endurance and perseverance. And to give thanks to the Father who made His people fit for the inheritance. It is a prayer for a whole transformed life — and every part of it flows from the gospel statement Paul lands on at the end: the Father delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have our redemption, the forgiveness of our sins. The walk worthy of the Lord is the fruit; the transfer into the kingdom of the Son is the root. This week teaches a man to pray Paul’s prayer for the kind of life the gospel makes possible.

sections.heading: WHAT WE ARE GOING AFTER
paras: This week goes after the connection between knowing and walking — between the inner filling Paul prays for and the outer life it produces. Many men want to know God’s will as information, a map for decisions. Paul prays for the knowledge of God’s will as a filling that produces a worthy walk — fruit in every good work, growth in knowing God, strength for endurance, and overflowing thankfulness. The knowing he prays for is not data for the head; it is a fullness that reshapes the feet. To know God’s will, in Paul’s sense, is to be so filled with God that one’s whole manner of life changes.

The goal this week is to pray for the kind of life that flows from the gospel, and to see clearly that it flows — it is fruit, not root. Paul prays for the worthy walk, the good works, the endurance, the thankfulness — and then grounds it all in the transfer from darkness into the kingdom of the beloved Son. The order is the order of every gospel week: first the rescue, then the walk; first the redemption, then the fruit. A man does not walk worthy to be transferred into the kingdom; he walks worthy because he has been. The prayer asks God to grow the fruit of a salvation already given.

sections.heading: WHY START HERE
paras: Because a forgiven man, having learned to pray for sight, now needs to pray for the life that sight produces — and to keep the gospel order straight while he does. The danger is that prayers for a holy life quietly slide back into law: pleading for a worthy walk as the price of acceptance rather than the fruit of it. Paul’s prayer guards against this by grounding every petition in the finished transfer into the kingdom of the Son. Week Four is here to teach a man to pray boldly for a transformed life — fruitful, strong, thankful — while resting the whole time on the redemption already accomplished.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Filled, to Walk Worthy
paras: Paul’s central request is that the Colossians would be filled with the knowledge of God’s will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding. The word filled is generous — not a trickle of guidance but a flooding, a saturation. And the knowledge of God’s will here is not mainly about decisions — which job, which house — but about the will of God for a man’s character and life: who God is calling him to be and how God is calling him to live. Paul prays that this would fill a man so completely that it overflows into wisdom and understanding for the actual living of his days.

And the purpose is immediately stated: that you may walk worthily of the Lord, to please him in all respects. The filling is for the walking. Paul never prays for knowledge that stays in the head; he prays for knowledge that reaches the feet. To walk worthy of the Lord does not mean to earn His favor — the gospel settled that — but to live a life that fits the gospel, that matches the dignity of a son, that pleases the Father the way a beloved child’s life pleases a good father. Not to win love, but as the natural response of one already loved.

Then Paul unfolds what the worthy walk looks like in four phrases that are worth praying by name: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God, strengthened with all power, and giving thanks to the Father. Fruitfulness, deeper knowing, strength, and gratitude — a whole portrait of a thriving Christian life. The man in the dust, whose life feels barren and weak and joyless, is praying for exactly the opposite: fruit where there was barrenness, knowing where there was distance, strength where there was exhaustion, thanks where there was complaint. And all of it asked for, not achieved.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Strengthened, and Transferred

heads.text: JOHN CALVIN — the hand that digs up the treasure

paras: Paul prays that they would be strengthened with all power, according to the might of his glory — and then names what the strength is for, which is surprising. Not for triumph or conquest, but for all endurance and perseverance with joy. The strength Paul asks God to supply is the strength to keep going, to bear up under what does not change, to be patient when relief does not come — and to do it with joy. This is the strength the man in the dust most needs: not the power to escape his hard season, but the power to endure it without being crushed, and even to find joy in it. Resurrection power, last week, was aimed at change; here the same power is aimed at endurance. Both are gifts of God, asked for in prayer.

And then Paul grounds the entire prayer in the gospel, with one of the great salvation statements in Scripture: giving thanks to the Father, who made us fit to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light, who delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have our redemption, the forgiveness of our sins. Read the verbs: made fit, delivered, translated. All past tense, all God’s doing, all already accomplished. The man did not make himself fit; the Father did. He did not escape the darkness; he was delivered. He did not earn his way into the kingdom; he was transferred, carried, relocated by grace.

This is why the whole prayer rests easy. Paul can pray boldly for a worthy walk, fruitfulness, strength, and thanksgiving precisely because none of it is the price of the kingdom — all of it is the fruit of a transfer already made. The man is already in the kingdom of the beloved Son. He already has redemption and the forgiveness of sins. So the worthy walk is not a frantic effort to get in; it is the glad life of one who is already inside. And the prayer ends where every gospel week ended: in thanksgiving to the Father who did it all. A man filled with the knowledge of that will walk worthy — not to be saved, but because he is.

Calvin gave prayer the longest chapter in the Institutes, and his governing image fits this week exactly: the gospel has laid up an immense treasure in Christ, and prayer is how a man digs it up. Everything Paul asks for in Colossians 1 — knowledge, wisdom, strength, endurance — is already the believer’s in Christ. Prayer is the hand that goes and gets it. Calvin’s four rules function as a diagnostic here: reverence, a sincere sense of want, humble submission, and confident hope. Most men are strong in two and weak in two. Read Paul’s prayer and notice which of the four your own praying habitually skips. What Christ purchased for you does not become yours by being admired. It becomes yours by being asked for. So prayer is the honest speech of a forgiven man — collecting what was already bought in his name.

stations.verse: For this cause, we also, since the day we heard this, don’t cease praying and making requests for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,
note: Two things stand out. First, the persistence: don’t cease praying. Paul prayed for these believers continually, without quitting, though many he had never met. Real intercession is unceasing labor, not a passing mention. Second, the request: to be filled with the knowledge of God’s will — saturated, flooded, not merely informed. Paul wants for them a fullness of knowing God’s will that produces wisdom for actual living. This is the prayer to pray for a man you love: not that his path would be easy, but that he would be filled with the knowledge of God’s will.
stations.question: Is there anyone you pray for “without ceasing” — and what would it look like to pray, persistently, that they would be filled with the knowledge of God’s will?
stations.gloss: to fill, to fill up completely, to fill to the full, to saturate. Paul does not pray for a measure of knowledge but for a filling — the believer flooded full with the knowledge of God’s will, leaving no empty room.
stations.live: Each morning this week, before you check your phone, ask God to fill you with the knowledge of His will for that day — and then go do the first ordinary thing well.
body: Because the prayer is for plēroō — a complete filling — it assumes the knowledge of God’s will is meant to occupy the whole man, not sit in a corner of his mind. A life filled to the full with God’s will has been crowded out of room for the dust. God does not want to inform a corner of your mind. He wants to fill you full — until there is no empty room left for the dust.
The man in the dust, half-empty and easily filled with worry, is prayed for here: to be filled to the full with the knowledge of God’s will.
